catalog_quote: [p. 58] 3.2.1.1 TONES high plain /+̀/ high creaky /+́/ low /+/ high stop /+'/ weak /ə/ For /+̄/, the 'Ìn-θà mid', see §3.2.2. ... 3.2.2 PHONEME DESCRIPTION These are as in SB except as set out below: Tones are on the whole similar to SB tones, but there are differences between the intonation patterns of IT and those of SB, which are of course matched by differences in the realisation of syllable tone, especially at the end of a sentence, and sometimes at the end of a clause. The difference is so marked in the case of a small number of sentence-final and clause-final particles (curiously, not all are so affected), that it proved impossible to assign any of the usual phonemic tones to them. These particles are therefore marked in the texts and examples with a macron: /+̄/. This is to be understood as representing the pitch and voice-quality features associated with SB /+̀/ or /+́/ ... also, though perhaps less often, like SB /+/, and sometimes with the held level mid pitch so characteristic of Ìn-θà speech. The particles so marked are IT /wā (wɔ̄), mā (mɔ̄), shɔ̄, lɔ̄, lɛ̄/. [p. 69] 3.3.2.2 WEAKENING Weakening occurs in IT much as in SB, though there are indications that it is less used. For example: ... /nà-wɛ'/ ... ear ... In a few words the weak vowel has apparently been dropped, leaving a fusion of the initials on either side of it: ... And in other words the entire weak syllable is omitted:

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (218 pp., Bradley ed. 1995, PL A-83; footer 'Online edition licensed 2015 CC BY-SA 4.0') and its text; rendered book pp. 56, 58, 67, 69 (PDF pages 68, 70, 79, 81) and read them as images. Both prose quotes are verbatim: p. 58 §3.2.2 'These are as in SB except as set out below: Tones are on the whole similar to SB tones, but there are differences between the intonation patterns of IT and those of SB.. that it proved impossible to assign any of the usual phonemic tones to them.' and p. 69 §3.3.2.2 'Weakening occurs in IT much as in SB, though there are indications that it is less used.' ( lines 3383-3390 and 3892). Minor difference: the tone table (p. 58 §3.2.1.1) in the PDF uses a '+'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Intha is described as a tone language with the Standard Burmese system (three tones on open/nasal syllables, a stopped syllable type, and a 'weak' toneless schwa syllable); the only prominence-related phenomenon described is 'weakening', i.e. reduction of non-final syllables to /ə/ as in Standard Burmese, said to be somewhat less used in Intha. No word-stress placement rule is stated anywhere in the Intha section; the word 'stress' does not occur in Okell's paper.
new_statements.exceptions: Some sentence-final and clause-final particles (/wa (wo), ma (mo), sho, lo, le/) cannot be assigned a phonemic tone and are marked with a macron; in some words the weak syllable is dropped entirely or fused (p. 69).
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable tone described at word and sentence level from recorded narratives (Ywa-ma village, west bank of Inle Lake, 1961 and 1969); weakening concerns non-final syllables of polysyllabic words. Tone symbols in the quote were rendered from the PDF's diacritics (acute = high plain/creaky per the volume's conventions; the text garbles them as 1+1).
new_statements.identity_note: Okell 1995 describes Intha (IT) of Ywa-ma and neighbouring west-bank villages of Inle Lake (Nyaungshwe), recorded 1961 and 1969; Danu (the other half of Glottolog's inth1238) is not described there (Bradley's preface calls Danu and Taungyo 'virtually undescribed'). The Khin Sandar Toe 2018 article concerns Danu of the Nawnghkio area (vocabulary only). Naksuk 2012/2014 describe Intha of Inle Lake, Nyaung Shwe Township.

new_statements.quote: There are four contrastive tones in Intha phonology: /1, 2, 3, 4/. These four tones function in both major and minor syllables. In presyllables, the tone exists at the phonetic level, usually in mid tone [33]. However, it is neither significant nor contrastive at the phonemic level. [...] There are four tones: /1/ low-falling, /2/ low-rising-falling, /3/ mid-rising-falling, and /4/ high-falling.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing Okell 1995 statement (tone language, no stress statement): both describe Intha as tonal with reduced/weak presyllables and neither states a word-stress rule. Naksuk counts four tones where Okell counts five (Okell's 'weak' /ə/ syllable type is treated by Naksuk as the toneless presyllable), a difference in the tone inventory, not in stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Intha is described as a four-tone language (low-falling [21], low-rising-falling [232], mid-rising-falling [343], high-falling [54ʔ]); tone is contrastive on major and minor syllables but only phonetic (mid [33]) and non-contrastive on presyllables. The words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere in the article. Every phonetic transcription puts a primary-stress mark [ˈ] on the (single) full syllable, e.g. /ca2/ [ˈtɕaː232] 'tiger', /cɔ4/ [ˈtɕɔ54ʔ] 'stone' (pp. 192, 203), which implicitly treats the full/major syllable as the prominent one and the presyllable as reduced, but no rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: none; eastern vs western Intha differ in the realisation of some vowels under tone /4/ (p. 208), not in prominence
new_statements.identity_note: Naksuk 2014 (and the 2012 thesis) is based on two informants, one from the eastern and one from the western side of Inle Lake (Nyaung Shwe Township), collected 2010-2011; Okell 1995 is the Intha of the same Inle Lake area. No other variety is described.

tone_statements.quote: 声調 (T) /ˍ(符号なし), ˋ, ˊ, ˍ(ʔ)/ ... 声調型は次のとおり。I. /ˍ/ [22] 低平・長。II. /ˋ/ [442] 高降・長。III. /ˊ/ [ˀ42~ˀ44] 高降または高平・短・緩い緊喉。IV. /ˍ(ʔ)/ [ˀ22] 低平・短・堅い緊喉。軽声音節は /ə/ で表わす。なお，文末の第III声は，しばしば心もち長めに発音される傾向がある（間投助詞に多く観察される）。
tone_statements.translation: Tones (T): /unmarked, grave, acute, unmarked+(ʔ)/ ... The tone types are as follows. I. /unmarked/ [22] low level, long. II. /grave/ [442] high falling, long. III. /acute/ [ˀ42~ˀ44] high falling or high level, short, lax glottal constriction. IV. /(ʔ)/ [ˀ22] low level, short, tight glottal constriction. Light (weak) syllables are written with /ə/. Note that sentence-final tone III often tends to be pronounced slightly longer (frequently observed on interjectional particles).

tone_statements.summary: Danu: 4 syllable-tone types on the Burmese pattern — low level [22], high falling [442], short creaky/lax-glottal high [ˀ42~ˀ44], short stopped [ˀ22] — plus toneless weak /ə/ syllables; syllable TBU.

sources.note: No use of the word 'stress' for Intha. Tone inventory (p. 58): high plain, high creaky, low, high stop, weak /ə/. 'Tones are on the whole similar to SB tones' with intonation differences at sentence/clause end; some final particles cannot be assigned a phonemic tone (p. 58). 'Weakening occurs in IT much as in SB, though there are indications that it is less used' (p. 69), i.e. reduced schwa syllables in non-final position as in Standard Burmese. No word-stress rule stated.

sources.note: Primary tone-marked data, no prose analysis: each Danu form carries Chao-style superscripts (e.g. tjaɪʔ² 'to grind', pè⁴ 'left (hand)', nã⁴ 'bad smell', mwé² 'fragrant'), i.e. Luce recorded pitch level and glottal/stop phonation per word, with stopped rhymes (-ʔ²) grouped in their own columns — usable for Danu tone-category correspondences with Written Burmese.
